Título II, Sección 201(a): "Todas las personas tendrán derecho al disfrute pleno e igualitario de los bienes, servicios, instalaciones, privilegios, ventajas y alojamientos de cualquier lugar de alojamiento público, según se define en esta sección, sin discriminación ni segregación por motivos de raza, color, religión u origen nacional."

Usando estos extractos y su conocimiento de la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964, construya una respuesta que (1) explique las campañas específicas del movimiento y los actos de desobediencia civil (US.72–US.74) que proporcionaron el impulso moral y político directo para que el Congreso aprobara la Ley de Derechos Civiles, (2) analice la importancia de incluir el 'sexo' como categoría protegida en el Título VII — incluyendo las circunstancias controvertidas bajo las cuales se añadió — y (3) evalúe las limitaciones de la Ley para abordar la discriminación electoral, conectando esta brecha con la necesidad de la Ley de Derechos de Voto de 1965 (US.77). items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 represented the legislative culmination of a decade of direct-action campaigns but contained a critical enforcement gap around voting rights that made a separate statute necessary the following year. Title VII's inclusion of 'sex' was added by Virginia Representative Howard W. Smith, a segregationist who hoped it would make the bill so broad it would fail — ironically creating the legal foundation for decades of women's employment rights litigation. The Act's Title I addressed voting discrimination only indirectly (literacy tests in federal elections); it did not address the full range of voter registration obstacles — poll taxes, intimidation, discriminatory local administration — that disenfranchised Black Southerners. The 24th Amendment (1964) eliminated federal poll taxes but left state elections unaddressed. Fannie Lou Hamer's 1964 DNC testimony illustrated the ongoing violence and intimidation in voter registration. REASONING: Should explain how the limits of Title I made the comprehensive voting protections of the Voting Rights Act of 1965's Section 5 (preclearance) necessary.

Extended Response — Knowledge Synthesis — TENNESSEE CONNECTION

No source is provided for this item. Draw on your knowledge of the Civil Rights Movement to answer the following question.

Tennessee played a distinctive role in the Civil Rights Movement: the Highlander Folk School (Monteagle, TN) trained generations of civil rights activists; the Nashville sit-in campaign produced some of the movement's most important leaders; and Tennessee's urban centers were among the first Southern cities to achieve peaceful desegregation. Using your knowledge of these Tennessee connections and the broader Civil Rights Movement, construct a multi-paragraph extended argument that addresses the following question: To what extent did the organizing and leadership models developed in Tennessee — particularly in Nashville — shape the national strategy of the Civil Rights Movement?

Your argument must (1) identify and explain at least two specific ways that the Nashville model of nonviolent direct action (developed through Lawson's workshops and the sit-in campaign of 1960) was more systematically philosophical than other early sit-in movements (such as Greensboro), (2) analyze how the Nashville student leadership — including Diane Nash, John Lewis, and James Bevel — exported the Nashville model to national organizations (SNCC) and campaigns (Freedom Rides, Selma), (3) evaluate the role of the Highlander Folk School as a training ground that connected earlier labor and civil rights movements (pre-1960) to the sit-in generation, and (4) assess whether the success of Nashville's model reflected Tennessee-specific conditions or a universally transferable approach. Use the CER framework.

Respuesta Extendida — Síntesis de Conocimiento — CONEXIÓN CON TENNESSEE

No se proporciona ninguna fuente para este ítem. Recurra a su conocimiento del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles para responder la siguiente pregunta.

Tennessee jugó un papel distintivo en el Movimiento de Derechos Civiles: la Escuela Highlander Folk (Monteagle, TN) entrenó a generaciones de activistas de derechos civiles; la campaña de sentadas de Nashville produjo algunos de los líderes más importantes del movimiento; y los centros urbanos de Tennessee fueron de los primeros en el Sur en lograr la desegregación pacífica. Usando su conocimiento de estas conexiones con Tennessee y el Movimiento de Derechos Civiles más amplio, construya un argumento extendido de varios párrafos que aborde la siguiente pregunta: ¿En qué medida los modelos de organización y liderazgo desarrollados en Tennessee — particularmente en Nashville — dieron forma a la estrategia nacional del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles?

Su argumento debe (1) identificar y explicar al menos dos formas específicas en que el modelo de acción directa no violenta de Nashville (desarrollado a través de los talleres de Lawson y la campaña de sentadas de 1960) fue más sistemáticamente filosófico que otros movimientos de sentadas tempranos (como Greensboro), (2) analizar cómo el liderazgo estudiantil de Nashville — incluyendo a Diane Nash, John Lewis y James Bevel — exportó el modelo de Nashville a organizaciones nacionales (SNCC) y campañas (Viajes de la Libertad, Selma), (3) evaluar el papel de la Escuela Highlander Folk como campo de entrenamiento que conectó los movimientos laborales y de derechos civiles anteriores (antes de 1960) con la generación de las sentadas, y (4) evaluar si el éxito del modelo de Nashville reflejó condiciones específicas de Tennessee o un enfoque universalmente transferible. Use el marco CER.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM: The Nashville model of nonviolent direct action was the most systematically developed and philosophically grounded approach to civil rights protest in the early 1960s, and the leadership it produced — particularly Nash, Lewis, and Bevel — became the primary carriers of that model to national organizations and campaigns, making Tennessee's contribution to the movement disproportionate to its size and political environment. NASHVILLE'S DISTINCTIVENESS vs. GREENSBORO (at least 2): (1) Philosophical systematicity — The Greensboro sit-in (February 1, 1960) was an act of spontaneous courage by four A&T students with no formal nonviolent training; the Nashville students had been training weekly with James Lawson since fall 1959, studying Gandhi's philosophy in India, Thoreau's civil disobedience, and Christian nonresistance — making Nashville's action a deliberate application of a developed theoretical framework. (2) Organizational infrastructure — Nashville had a pre-existing carpooling and communication network (modeled on the MBB), a coordinated economic boycott targeting downtown merchants, and a legal defense team (Z. Alexander Looby); Greensboro lacked these elements, making Nashville's campaign more structurally complete. EXPORT OF NASHVILLE MODEL: Diane Nash co-founded SNCC at Shaw University (April 1960), bringing the Nashville training framework into SNCC's founding philosophy. When the original CORE Freedom Riders were attacked and burned out in Anniston and Birmingham (May 1961), Nash organized Nashville students to continue the rides despite the violence — demonstrating the 'fill the jails' philosophy. John Lewis became SNCC chairman (1963) and helped organize the March on Washington; he led the Selma march across the Edmund Pettus Bridge on Bloody Sunday (March 7, 1965). James Bevel became SCLC's director of nonviolent education and organized the Birmingham Children's Crusade (1963). HIGHLANDER FOLK SCHOOL: Located in Monteagle, TN (later removed to Knoxville after losing its charter), Highlander was the primary training ground connecting the labor movement (CIO organizing in the 1930s-40s) to the civil rights movement. Rosa Parks attended Highlander in summer 1955, weeks before her arrest; Septima Clark developed the Citizenship Schools there; Myles Horton's interracial workshops in the 1950s directly trained participants in the 1955-1960 wave of civil rights activity. UNIVERSALITY vs. TENNESSEE-SPECIFIC: Students should argue both sides — Nashville's specific conditions (Fisk, Vanderbilt, Meharry, and Tennessee A&I as concentrated HBCU and university community; sympathetic local press; relatively moderate Nashville business community) created favorable conditions; but the framework itself (nonviolent training + economic pressure + moral confrontation) was successfully exported to Albany, Birmingham, Selma, and Mississippi.

Extended Response — Knowledge Synthesis

No source is provided for this item. Draw on your knowledge of U.S. History to answer the following question.

The Civil Rights Movement achieved two landmark legislative victories — the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 — within an eighteen-month period. Yet historians debate whether these laws represented the culmination of the movement or a transition point after which the movement's goals shifted and fragmented. Using your knowledge of the Civil Rights Movement (US.71–US.77) and its aftermath, construct a multi-paragraph extended argument that addresses the following question: Did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 represent the fulfillment of the Civil Rights Movement's goals or a foundation that revealed the limits of legal reform?

Your argument must (1) explain what specific goals the movement had articulated by 1963–1965 (drawing on the demands of the March on Washington, the SNCC voter registration campaigns, and the Selma campaigns), (2) analyze what the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 actually accomplished — including the structural mechanisms (EEOC, preclearance, federal examiners) that gave them enforcement power, (3) evaluate what the laws left unaddressed — specifically the economic inequality, housing segregation, and Northern de facto segregation that fell outside the laws' scope, and (4) reach a reasoned conclusion about whether the 1964–1965 legislation was a fulfillment, a foundation, or both — and what this debate reveals about the relationship between legal equality and substantive equality in American history. Use the CER framework.

Respuesta Extendida — Síntesis de Conocimiento

No se proporciona ninguna fuente para este ítem. Recurra a su conocimiento de la Historia de los EE. UU. para responder la siguiente pregunta.

El Movimiento de Derechos Civiles logró dos victorias legislativas históricas — la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964 y la Ley de Derechos de Voto de 1965 — en un período de dieciocho meses. Sin embargo, los historiadores debaten si estas leyes representaron la culminación del movimiento o un punto de transición después del cual los objetivos del movimiento se desplazaron y fragmentaron. Usando su conocimiento del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles (US.71–US.77) y sus consecuencias, construya un argumento extendido de varios párrafos que aborde la siguiente pregunta: ¿La Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964 y la Ley de Derechos de Voto de 1965 representaron el cumplimiento de los objetivos del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles o una base que reveló los límites de la reforma legal?

Su argumento debe (1) explicar qué objetivos específicos había articulado el movimiento para 1963–1965 (recurriendo a las demandas de la Marcha sobre Washington, las campañas de registro de votantes del SNCC y las campañas de Selma), (2) analizar qué lograron realmente la Ley de Derechos Civiles de 1964 y la Ley de Derechos de Voto de 1965 — incluyendo los mecanismos estructurales (EEOC, preclearance, examinadores federales) que les dieron poder de aplicación, (3) evaluar lo que las leyes dejaron sin abordar — específicamente la desigualdad económica, la segregación de vivienda y la segregación de facto del Norte que quedó fuera del alcance de las leyes, y (4) llegar a una conclusión razonada sobre si la legislación de 1964–1965 fue un cumplimiento, una base o ambas cosas — y qué revela este debate sobre la relación entre la igualdad legal y la igualdad sustantiva en la historia estadounidense. Use el marco CER.
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (4/4) response would include: CLAIM: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 fulfilled the movement's core legal and political goals — desegregation of public accommodations and restoration of voting rights — but their passage immediately exposed the deeper economic and structural inequalities that legal equality alone could not address, revealing that the movement had always contained goals that exceeded what legislation could achieve. MOVEMENT GOALS BY 1963–65: The March on Washington was officially the 'March for Jobs and Freedom' — A. Philip Randolph's framing included a $2/hour minimum wage, a federal jobs program, and fair housing alongside civil rights legislation. SNCC voter registration campaigns in Mississippi (Freedom Summer, 1964) targeted the fundamental exclusion of Black Southerners from political power. The Selma campaign was explicitly focused on the gap between the 15th Amendment's nominal guarantee and the reality of Black voter registration in Selma (2% registration in Dallas County despite Black majority). WHAT THE LAWS ACCOMPLISHED: CRA 1964 — desegregated public accommodations (Title II), prohibited employment discrimination (Title VII), created EEOC as enforcement mechanism, cut off federal funding to segregated institutions (Title VI). VRA 1965 — suspended literacy tests in covered jurisdictions (Section 4), created preclearance requirement (Section 5), authorized federal voter examiners, produced dramatic increases in Black voter registration in covered states. WHAT THE LAWS LEFT UNADDRESSED: Neither law addressed housing segregation (Fair Housing Act would not come until 1968); neither addressed economic inequality (poverty rates, wage gaps, wealth gaps). Northern de facto segregation — school segregation through residential patterns rather than law — was not covered by CRA. King's 1966 Chicago campaign exposed the limits of nonviolent direct action and federal legislation in addressing Northern housing discrimination (redlining, restrictive covenants, real estate steering). The Poor People's Campaign (1968) reflected King's recognition that legal equality had not produced economic equality. CONCLUSION: Students should argue that 'foundation' is more accurate than 'fulfillment' — the laws ended the legal framework of Jim Crow but could not self-execute on economic justice; they created the infrastructure (EEOC, voting rights enforcement) for ongoing struggle but did not resolve the deeper structural questions the movement had always contained. The distinction between formal/legal equality and substantive/economic equality is key.
